explanations: luna: The verse challenges disbelief by reminding people that after life and death they will be returned to God (ثُمَّ إِلَيْهِ تُرْجَعُونَ); disbelief cannot cancel the return.

luna: The source-section root و ج ه is used here: The one who submits his face to God (أَسْلَمَ وَجْهَهُ لِلَّهِ) supplies the positive pole to turning away: orientation can embody submission. | terra: One who submits his face to God and does good has reward and security; willing face-direction supplies the positive reverse of turning away.

luna: The source-section root و ج ه is defined through the place one faces; wherever you turn, there is the Face of God (فَأَيْنَمَا تُوَلُّوا فَثَمَّ وَجْهُ اللَّهِ). | terra: Wherever people turn (تُوَلُّوا), there is God's face; the directional sense of the root shows spatial turning cannot place anyone outside the divine relation.

luna: The source-section's root و ل ي with عن means turning away and leaving nearness; this verse asks what turned people away from their qibla (مَا وَلَّاهُمْ عَن قِبْلَتِهِمْ), an especially close parallel. | terra: The question “what turned them from their direction?” uses the same turning root for a change of qiblah, clarifying the spatial branch beside moral turning away.

luna: The qibla passage says some will turn back on their heels (يَنقَلِبُ عَلَىٰ عَقِبَيْهِ); the ayah's own contribution is the reversal from following the Messenger when tested. | terra: The change of qiblah distinguishes one who follows the Messenger from one who turns back on his heels; literal direction exposes moral reversal.

luna: The source-section root و ج ه appears as the Prophet turns his face toward the Sacred Mosque (فَوَلِّ وَجْهَكَ), a concrete qibla scene for the face-as-direction gloss. | terra: God observes the Prophet's face turning toward heaven and appoints a pleasing direction, repeatedly commanding him to turn his face toward the Sacred Mosque; face and turning function as literal orientation.

luna: The source-section root و ج ه is explicit in “for each is a direction toward which it turns” (وِجْهَةٌ هُوَ مُوَلِّيهَا); the verse then directs people toward good deeds. | terra: Each community has a direction (وجهة) toward which it turns, yet wherever people are God will bring them all together; chosen orientation and unavoidable arrival meet in one ayah.

luna: The source-section root و ج ه is used here: The qibla instruction continues: wherever the Prophet goes out, he must turn his face toward the Sacred Mosque; this repeats the direction in 2:144. | terra: The repeated command to turn the face toward the Sacred Mosque confirms that وَجْه and the turning root can jointly describe concrete direction.

luna: The source-section root و ج ه is used here: The same direction is required wherever the believers come from, so that people have no argument against them; it completes the qibla scene with its boundary. | terra: The qiblah command is extended to every location: all are to turn their faces toward it, a collective use of orientation distinct from rejection.
terra: Those struck by affliction confess that they belong to God and are returning to Him; recognition freely anticipates the universal return.
terra: Followers under punishment wish for another return so they might disown their leaders; the desired return exists only as regret once the consequences appear.

luna: The source-section root و ج ه appears in a boundary: righteousness is not simply turning faces east or west (تُوَلُّوا وُجُوهَكُمْ), so outward direction alone is not the measure. | terra: Righteousness is not the mere turning of faces east or west; the ayah marks the boundary between physical orientation and the moral turning at issue in 88:23.

luna: The source-section root ء ت ي appears in the judgment scene of God coming to people in canopies of cloud with angels; it is a distinct arrival. | terra: Those who hold back are asked whether they await God and the angels coming and the matter being decided; decisive arrival closes deliberation.

luna: The warning says people will be returned to God and each soul paid for what it earned (تُرْجَعُونَ فِيهِ إِلَى اللَّهِ); no one can turn away from that accounting. | terra: People are warned of a day when they will be returned to God and every soul will be paid in full for what it earned; return and account are stated as one sequence.
terra: After listing the attractions of the nearer life, the ayah says that with God is the good مَآب; worldly objects are set against the enduring return-place.
terra: After asking whether they will submit, the ayah says that if they turn away the Messenger's duty is only delivery; direction of response is left to the hearers.
luna: A party given scripture turns away (يَتَوَلَّىٰ) when called to God's Book for judgment; the ayah joins turning away to refusal of an arriving decision.
luna: People are gathered for a Day of no doubt and each soul is fully paid for what it earned; it directly parallels return followed by account.
luna: All in the heavens and earth submit to God willingly or unwillingly, and to Him they return; it states both chosen and unavoidable return in one ayah.

luna: On the Day faces become white or black (تَبْيَضُّ وُجُوهٌ وَتَسْوَدُّ وُجُوهٌ), a direct two-sided face scene parallel to al-Ghashiya's divided groups. | terra: On the Day when some faces whiten and others blacken, the face visibly registers two opposed outcomes, as it does in surah 88.

luna: The next ayah says the white-faced group is in God's mercy; it completes the favorable side introduced in 3:106. | terra: Those whose faces whiten abide in God's mercy, completing the favorable half of the face contrast in 3:106.
terra: After the Messenger's death, whoever turns back on his heels cannot harm God; departure changes the person, not the divine end or authority.
terra: People of the Book are warned to believe before faces are effaced and turned back upon their backs; face, reversal, and threatened judgment meet in one image.
terra: Death overtakes people wherever they are, even in fortified towers; no chosen place or direction prevents the decisive arrival.

luna: The source-section root و ل ي is used here: Whoever turns away from the Messenger is outside the Prophet's guardianship; the verse shares 88:21-22's limit on the messenger's role. | terra: Whoever turns away is outside the Messenger's charge, for he was not sent as their keeper; this closely matches reminder without control in 88:21-23.
terra: One who breaks with the Messenger is turned toward what he chose (نُوَلِّهِ مَا تَوَلَّى) and brought to Hell; chosen orientation becomes final destination.

luna: The source-section root و ج ه is used here: The best way is described as submitting one's face to God (أَسْلَمَ وَجْهَهُ لِلَّهِ) and following Abraham, again making face-direction a chosen allegiance. | terra: The best religion belongs to one who submits his face to God and does good, a positive orientation opposed to the face and back of refusal.
terra: Moses warns his people not to turn back on their backs lest they become losers; retreat is pictured as bodily reversal from a commanded destination.
terra: Obedience is commanded, but if people turn away the Messenger's obligation is only clear delivery, another exact formulation of the reminder's bounded role.
terra: All people's return is to God, who will inform them of what they did; the ayah directly binds return to disclosed deeds.

luna: A Lord's sign comes to them (تأتيهم), yet they turn away from it; this joins the image's arriving report to the refusal that follows. | terra: Whenever a sign from their Lord comes to them, they turn away from it; coming and abandonment of nearness form the repeated action.
luna: Truth came to them and was denied, then the reports they mocked will come to them (جاءهم ... يأتيهم); rejection does not prevent the later arrival.
terra: Standing before the Fire, they wish to be returned so they will no longer deny; arrival at punishment produces a return that is only a wish.
terra: God states that if they were returned they would resume what they were forbidden, revealing that mere reversal of location would not be genuine return to God.

luna: When the Hour comes suddenly, the deniers regret their neglect; this gives the sudden arrival in 12:107 its concrete consequence. | terra: Deniers of meeting God regret when the Hour comes suddenly and carry their burdens, joining unforeseen arrival to the denied meeting.
terra: The Prophet has none of his followers' account upon him, nor they his; it marks the boundary that explains why account belongs to God rather than the reminder.
terra: God knows what people earn, raises them by day until the term is fulfilled, then to Him is their return and disclosure; daily return rehearses final return.

luna: The source-section root و ج ه appears as Abraham directs his face toward the Creator (وَجَّهْتُ وَجْهِيَ), making bodily orientation an explicit turning toward God. | terra: Abraham says he has directed his face toward the Creator of heavens and earth; the face serves as an image of wholehearted chosen orientation.
terra: The ayah asks whether they await the angels, the Lord, or signs of the Lord to come, then warns that belief at that arrival will no longer benefit.
terra: Coming with a good deed or an evil deed produces distinct recompense, a broad counterpart to the lexicon's good and evil sides of coming.

luna: After declaring that each person bears their own burden, the verse says “to your Lord is your return” and He will inform you of your disagreements; return and account are adjacent. | terra: Each soul bears its own earning, then all return to their Lord and are informed of their disputes; individual responsibility culminates in return and account.
terra: Hell has a bed beneath its people and coverings above them; the plural غَوَاشٍ makes punitive envelopment a complete surrounding scene.
terra: When the Book's outcome arrives, deniers ask for intercession or a return so they can act differently; realized judgment closes the former choice.

luna: Night covers the day and pursues it rapidly; this is a recurring, ordinary covering that gives a concrete secondary sense to the source-section's Ghashiya image. | terra: God makes night cover day as each rapidly pursues the other, a repeated natural instance of the enveloping sense of غ ش و.
terra: The Children of Israel are tested with both good things and evil things so that they might return; the good-and-evil polarity serves voluntary return rather than fixing the final destination.

luna: The source-section root ء ت ي is used when the Hour comes upon people only suddenly (تَأْتِيكُمُ السَّاعَةُ إِلَّا بَغْتَةً), echoing the image's unexpected arrival. | terra: The Hour will come only suddenly; its hidden timing intensifies the section's sense of an arrival that cannot be managed by the one it reaches.
terra: At death the angels strike disbelievers' faces and backs, bringing the section's opposed bodily sides together at the beginning of return.
terra: Repentance is offered as good, but those who turn away are told they cannot frustrate God; their chosen departure cannot produce escape.
terra: The opponents are asked whether the news of earlier peoples has not come to them; the arrival of report carries warning through remembered outcomes.
terra: People offer excuses when the believers return to them, but they will themselves be returned to the Knower and informed of their deeds; a small return anticipates the final one.
terra: People are told to act because God, the Messenger, and believers will see, after which they are returned to the Knower and informed of their deeds.
luna: When a surah is revealed, some look at one another and then turn away (انصَرَفُوا); revelation arrives, but its hearers withdraw.

luna: After people are rescued at sea and then transgress, their return is to God, who informs them of their deeds; escape from danger does not alter the destination. | terra: After rescue, people transgress during the brief enjoyment of the nearer life; then their return is to God and He informs them of their deeds, closely matching the section's sequence.
terra: Those who do good receive the best, and neither darkness nor humiliation covers their faces; the negated covering defines the blessed side of the image.

luna: The source-section root غ ش و covers the faces of wrongdoers with pieces of dark night (أُغْشِيَتْ وُجُوهُهُمْ); it carries the covering image into the contrary face-state of judgment. | terra: Those who earn evil are covered with humiliation, and their faces seem covered by pieces of dark night; face, covering, and outcome meet directly.
luna: At the gathering, each soul faces what it did and is returned to God, its true Master; this makes the return a moment of disclosure.
terra: Whether the Prophet sees part of the threat or dies first, the opponents' return is to God, who witnesses their deeds; prophetic timing does not affect their destination.
terra: Worldly enjoyment is followed by return to God and severe punishment for disbelief, closely matching the little enjoyment, return, and punishment sequence developed in the prose.

luna: The source-section root و ج ه appears in the command to set one's face toward the upright religion (فَأَقِمْ وَجْهَكَ), a chosen religious orientation. | terra: The Prophet is commanded to set his face to the religion as a monotheist, making face-direction a continuing religious stance.
terra: The truth has come from the Lord; each person's guidance or error is his own, and the Prophet is not their keeper, linking arrival of truth to free response.
terra: People are told to seek forgiveness and return penitently for good provision; if they turn away, a great day's punishment is feared, setting the two orientations against each other.
terra: People fold their breasts and cover themselves to hide, yet God knows what they conceal and reveal; turning and covering fail to escape divine knowledge before account.
terra: Hud commands repentance and asks his people not to turn away as criminals; voluntary return and culpable departure are made explicit alternatives.
terra: Hud says he has delivered the message; if they turn away, God can replace them and they cannot harm Him, showing their turning changes neither the message nor divine power.
luna: Shuʿayb says “to Him I turn” (وَإِلَيْهِ أُنِيبُ), a personal example of voluntary turning toward God.

luna: The source-section root ء ت ي is used for the Hour coming suddenly while its people are unaware (تَأْتِيهِمُ السَّاعَةُ بَغْتَةً), pairing two arrivals as the commentary does. | terra: This ayah itself sets two arrivals side by side: a covering punishment (غاشية) may come to them, or the Hour may come suddenly; it exactly unfolds the section's reading of 88:1.

luna: The same night-covering of day recurs here; its ordinary cycle contrasts with the overwhelming cover of the source image. | terra: Night covering day is repeated in a creation context, preserving the ordinary covering sense beside the idiom of a coming affliction.

luna: God guides those who turn back to Him (مَن أَنَابَ إِلَيْهِ), a specific voluntary return matching the source-section's awāb branch. | terra: God guides to Himself whoever turns penitently, stating the voluntary divineward movement that the section derives from أَوَّاب.
terra: Those who believe and do right have joy and a good مَآب, explicitly naming the favorable return-place.
terra: The Prophet says he was commanded to worship God, calls to Him, and that to Him is his مَآب; mission, direction, and return share one endpoint.
terra: The Messenger's charge is only delivery while the reckoning belongs to God, precisely matching the movement from “you are only a reminder” to “upon Us is their account.”
terra: Messengers ask earlier nations whether the news of those before them has not come, another direct scene in which news arrives to its hearers.
terra: When punishment comes, wrongdoers ask for a short delay so they may answer the call and follow messengers; arrival makes the formerly voluntary response unavailable.
terra: Fire covers their faces, combining the section's face with the punitive sense of an overwhelming covering.

luna: The source-section root ء ت ي appears in God's command has come (أَتَىٰ أَمْرُ اللَّهِ); people are told not to hasten it, making arrival certain while human timing remains limited. | terra: God's command is spoken of as already having come and people are told not to hasten it; prophetic perfect makes the future arrival certain.
luna: The source-section root ء ت ي appears as God comes upon the plotters' building from its foundations; this is a distinct punitive arrival.
terra: The wrongdoers await only the angels or their Lord's command to come; arrival marks the end of their present choice.
terra: Plotters are asked whether they feel secure from punishment coming from where they do not perceive, preserving the image of unnoticed threatening arrival.
terra: If they turn away, the Messenger's task is only clear delivery, matching the stance from which 88:21 addresses the Prophet.
luna: Each person's record is attached to them and brought forth as an open book on Resurrection Day; this begins a concrete account scene after the source's return.
luna: The person is told to read the book, with oneself sufficient as reckoner (حَسِيبًا); the source-section's root ح س ب is directly present.
terra: God knows the inner self and is forgiving to the أَوَّابِين, those who repeatedly return; voluntary return is grounded in inward rectitude and forgiveness.
terra: When the one God is mentioned in the Quran, the hearers turn their backs in aversion; moral refusal is staged as the bodily back-turning developed by the section.

luna: When given ease, a person turns away and withdraws to his side, but in hardship despairs; this gives a specific reversal between good arrival and turning away. | terra: When favored, the human turns away and withdraws to his side; the posture supplies the bodily scene underlying moral refusal.
terra: Those God leaves astray are gathered on their faces toward Hell, so the face that once chose orientation becomes the surface of compulsory movement.
luna: The Prophet is told not to let his eyes turn away from those who call on their Lord (وَلَا تَعْدُ عَيْنَاكَ عَنْهُمْ); this is a boundary against abandoning God-oriented companions.

luna: The laid-open record misses nothing, small or great, and the people find their deeds present; this is a specific account-scene parallel to 88:26. | terra: The record is placed, wrongdoers fear its contents, and nothing small or great is omitted; this expands what “upon Us is their account” entails.

luna: The verse condemns the person reminded of the Lord's signs who turns away from them (أَعْرَضَ عَنْهَا), echoing reminder followed by refusal. | terra: The person reminded of the Lord's signs then turns away and forgets what his hands sent ahead; present refusal is inseparable from the deeds awaiting account.
terra: Every being in the heavens and earth comes to the Merciful as a servant; universal coming strips away every claimed escape or independence.
terra: Between universal servanthood in 19:93 and each person's solitary coming in 19:95, God has counted every one exactly, joining return to reckoning.
terra: Every one of them will come to Him individually on Resurrection Day, a direct scene of the inevitable arrival implied by إِيَابَهُمْ.
terra: “Has the account of Moses come to you?” repeats the precise construction in which a report is represented as arriving to its hearer.
luna: The source-section root ء ت ي is used here: The Hour is coming and each soul will be recompensed for what it strives for; this joins arrival to the accounting that follows 88:25.

luna: The source-section root و ل ي names turning toward or away; Pharaoh is told that the one who lies and turns away (كَذَّبَ وَتَوَلَّىٰ) faces punishment. | terra: Moses and Aaron are told that punishment falls on whoever denies and turns away (كَذَّبَ وَتَوَلَّى), the exact moral pair behind 88:23-24.
terra: Pharaoh turns away, gathers his scheme, and then comes; literal departure followed by arrival makes the two motion verbs visible without yet naming final return.
terra: Whoever comes to his Lord as a criminal encounters Hell, giving the evil side of the section's statement that coming may bear good or evil.
terra: Whoever comes to Him as a believer with righteous deeds receives the highest ranks, completing the opposed good arrival begun in 20:74.
luna: The source-section root غ ش و names a coming-over that covers: here the sea overwhelms Pharaoh's pursuing army (فَغَشِيَهُم مِّنَ الْيَمِّ مَا غَشِيَهُمْ), a concrete destructive arrival.

luna: Whoever turns away from the reminder (أَعْرَضَ عَنْهُ) will bear a burden on Resurrection Day, directly joining refusal to later judgment. | terra: Whoever turns away from God's reminder will carry a burden on Resurrection Day, directly joining rejection of reminder to the final consequence.

luna: That burden remains with them on the Day of Resurrection; this completes 20:100's consequence for turning away. | terra: The turner of 20:100 remains under that burden, which is an evil load on Resurrection Day; this gives the enduring outcome of the refusal.
terra: Faces are humbled before the Living, Self-Sustaining One; their Day-of-Judgment orientation conveys the submission that cannot then be refused.

luna: Turning away from God's reminder (أَعْرَضَ عَن ذِكْرِي) is followed by a constricted life, a specific consequence for the image's act of turning away. | terra: Whoever turns from God's reminder receives a constricted life and is raised blind on Resurrection Day; worldly orientation issues in the condition of return.

luna: The source-section root ح س ب (accounting) meets its turning-away scene here: the account has drawn near while people are heedlessly turning away (مُّعْرِضُونَ). | terra: Humanity's reckoning has drawn near while they remain heedlessly turning away; impending account and present aversion are compressed into one sentence.
terra: Every soul tastes death, people are tested by evil and good, and to God they are returned; both kinds of coming experience terminate in the same return.
terra: The threatened event comes suddenly, confounds them, and cannot be repelled or delayed; its arrival removes every avenue of evasion.
terra: A destroyed town cannot return to earthly life, distinguishing the denied worldly return from the universal return to God.

luna: The source-section root و ج ه is used here: The person worshipping on an edge turns on his face when tested (انقَلَبَ عَلَىٰ وَجْهِهِ); the reversal ends in loss of both this life and the next. | terra: The person who worships on an edge reverses course on his face when trial comes; bodily orientation images a conditional commitment that fails under hardship.
terra: God grants a wrongdoing town respite, then seizes it, and to Him is the destination; delay cannot change where the reprieved finally arrives.
terra: Disbelievers remain in doubt until the Hour comes suddenly or the punishment of a barren day comes, giving two feared arrivals.

luna: Believers give while fearing because they are returning to their Lord (أَنَّهُم إِلَىٰ رَبِّهِمْ رَاجِعُونَ); return here produces humility rather than turning away. | terra: Believers give what they give while their hearts fear because they are returning to their Lord; awareness of return already directs present action.
luna: The people had the Lord's signs recited to them, yet turned back on their heels (تُنكَصُونَ); this gives a bodily reversal in response to reminder.
luna: The next ayah describes their arrogant, nighttime talk; it supplies the posture accompanying the turning back in 23:66.
terra: When death comes, the wrongdoer asks to be returned, locating the wish for voluntary amendment only after its opportunity has ended.
terra: The requested return is refused and a barrier remains until resurrection; compulsory forward movement replaces the return the person delayed.
luna: The question “did you think you would not be returned to Us?” (أَنَّكُمْ إِلَيْنَا لَا تُرْجَعُونَ) directly challenges denial of the destination asserted in 88:25.
luna: When called to God and the Messenger for judgment, a party turns away (مُّعْرِضُونَ); the ayah places refusal in a specific judgment scene.
luna: The next ayah contrasts that refusal: believers answer that they hear and obey when called to judgment, showing the positive response after 24:48.
terra: If people turn away, the Messenger bears only his assigned duty and his obligation is clear delivery; it parallels the reminder's bounded responsibility.

luna: On the day people are returned to God, He will tell them what they did (يَوْمَ يُرْجَعُونَ إِلَيْهِ فَيُنَبِّئُهُم); this directly parallels return followed by reckoning. | terra: God knows people's present position and, on the day they are returned to Him, will inform them of their deeds; no orientation is hidden from the final disclosure.
terra: Every renewed reminder that comes from the Merciful finds them turning away from it, directly coupling the coming reminder with the response in 88:23.
terra: Only the one who comes to God with a sound heart is saved; the quality of the voluntary coming determines the reception at the common destination.
terra: The condemned wish for another turn so they could become believers, defining compulsory arrival as the point beyond which willing return is unavailable.
terra: Noah says his followers' account rests only with his Lord, a direct prophetic statement of the division of responsibility found at the close of surah 88.
terra: Punishment comes to them suddenly while they do not perceive, preserving both unforeseen arrival and lack of awareness.
terra: Moses turns and flees without looking back when the staff moves, a literal fear-driven use of the bodily turn that differs from culpable aversion.
terra: Whoever comes with a good deed receives better and is safe from that Day's terror; moral content and the manner of arrival are directly joined.
terra: Whoever comes with an evil deed is cast face-first into the Fire; it supplies the evil arrival and also makes the face bear its outcome.
terra: The same staff scene again has Moses turn and flee without returning, confirming the literal motion sense and its nonmoral context.
terra: Pharaoh and his forces act arrogantly and suppose they will not be returned to God, voicing the false premise behind turning away.
terra: God seizes and casts them into the sea, overturning the supposition of 28:39 with an inescapable divine seizure.
terra: The one who comes with good receives better, while the one who comes with evil receives only what was done; arrival issues directly in account.
terra: Everything perishes except God's face, judgment belongs to Him, and to Him people are returned; face, account, and destination converge explicitly.

luna: Even in the painful case of parents urging their child to associate others with God, the return is to God, who will report the deeds; human ties do not change the final return. | terra: After the warning not to obey parents in association, God says that to Him is the return and He will inform people of what they did.

luna: The source-section root ء ت ي appears in the threat that punishment will surely come suddenly while they are unaware, a specific evil arrival. | terra: The hastened punishment has an appointed time and will surely come suddenly while they do not perceive.
terra: Punishment covers them from above and from beneath their feet, a direct punitive realization of the covering image.
luna: Every soul tastes death and then returns to God (ثُمَّ إِلَيْنَا تُرْجَعُونَ); death is a passage to the return, not an escape from it.
luna: God begins creation, repeats it, and people are then returned to Him; the verse connects return to the resurrection that makes judgment possible.

luna: The source-section root و ج ه appears in the command to set the face toward the upright religion (فَأَقِمْ وَجْهَكَ), developing orientation as a deliberate direction of life. | terra: Setting the face toward the upright religion turns a spatial image into stable moral orientation.
terra: Corruption is made manifest so people may taste part of what they have done “that they may return”; a nearer consequence is again an opening for voluntary return.

luna: The source-section root و ج ه appears in the command to set the face toward the upright religion before a day from God arrives that cannot be averted; chosen orientation stands against an unavoidable day. | terra: The command to set one's face toward the upright religion comes before a day arrives from God that cannot be turned back; voluntary orientation precedes irreversible arrival.
luna: The source-section root و ل ي is used here: The deaf cannot hear the call when they turn their backs and depart (تَوَلَّوْا مُدْبِرِينَ), a concrete refusal of a message.
terra: Even amid parental pressure toward association, the servant is told that the return is to God and He will inform everyone of their deeds; allegiance ends in disclosure.
terra: Submitting one's face to God while doing good is grasping the firmest handhold; chosen orientation creates nearness rather than abandoning it.

luna: After disbelief, their return is to God, who will inform them of their deeds (إِلَيْنَا مَرْجِعُهُمْ فَنُنَبِّئُهُم); the verse directly joins return to account. | terra: The Prophet is told not to grieve at disbelief: “to Us is their return,” and God will then inform them of what they did, reproducing the section's sequence and stance.

luna: The next ayah completes that sequence with brief enjoyment followed by being driven to severe punishment; its contribution is the fate after the return-and-report in 31:23. | terra: After 31:23's return, this ayah gives the brief worldly enjoyment followed by being driven into severe punishment; it shows the steps concealed between turning away and the final destination.
luna: The angel of death takes people, then they are returned to their Lord; this gives the return an explicit passage through death.
terra: Criminals before their Lord ask to be sent back so they can act rightly; their belated request contrasts with the still-open return sought by the lesser punishment in 32:21.
luna: The defiant are repeatedly sent back into the Fire when they try to leave it (أُعِيدُوا فِيهَا); this is a forced return to punishment beside the chosen return of 78:39.

luna: A lesser punishment comes before the greater one “so that they might return” (لَعَلَّهُمْ يَرْجِعُونَ); it supplies the interval in which turning back is still possible. | terra: The nearer punishment is distinguished from the greater punishment so that people may return; it makes explicit the section's claim that return remains voluntary before the final punishment.

luna: The one reminded of the Lord's signs then turns away (أَعْرَضَ عَنْهَا) and meets retribution, making the image's refusal and punishment explicit. | terra: No one is more unjust than the person reminded of the Lord's signs who then turns away; divine retribution follows the rejected reminder.
terra: Faces are turned about in the Fire while their owners regret obeying leaders rather than the Messenger; final facial motion exposes misdirected allegiance.
luna: Disbelievers claim the Hour will not come (لَا تَأْتِينَا السَّاعَةُ), directly opposing the source-section's root ء ت ي and its certainty of arrival.
terra: Mountains and birds are commanded to echo or repeatedly turn with David (أَوِّبِي), preserving the root's sense of responsive recurrence beyond human repentance.
terra: This repeated formulation says no sign from their Lord comes without their turning away, again joining arrival to deliberate aversion.
terra: The sudden cry leaves no time even for a bequest or return to one's family; earthly return to a familiar settlement is barred as final return begins.
terra: A single blast brings everyone together, present before God; the universal arrival is immediate and collective.
terra: After the gathering in 36:53, no soul is wronged and all are repaid for deeds, completing arrival with account.
terra: Abraham comes to his Lord with a sound heart; like 26:89, the arrival is inwardly prepared rather than merely compulsory.

luna: The source-section root ء و ب is used here: David is praised as “one who often returns” (أَوَّابٌ); this gives a Qur'anic example of the source's voluntary awāb sense. | terra: David is described as أَوَّاب, ever returning; the named root becomes a sustained quality of a servant rather than only the final return of all people.
terra: The gathered birds are described with the return root in relation to David; this responsive recurring movement is a distinct concrete shade of ء و ب.
terra: The news of the disputants is asked as something that has come to the Prophet, extending the “arriving report” formula from حديث to نبأ.
terra: David has nearness with God and a good مَآب, attaching the return-place to restored closeness after repentance.

luna: The source-section root ء و ب is used here: Solomon too is called “one who often returns” (أَوَّابٌ), extending the source's positive return-word to another servant of God. | terra: Solomon is praised as an excellent servant, أَوَّاب, repeating voluntary return as the defining quality of a prophet.
terra: Solomon has nearness with God and a good مَآب, again joining voluntary return to its favorable end.
terra: Job too is praised as an excellent servant, أَوَّاب, showing steadfast return through trial.
terra: The righteous are promised a good مَآب, stating one side of the opposed return-places developed in the section.
terra: The transgressors have an evil مَآب, reversing 38:49 with the same noun and clarifying that everyone returns but not to the same reception.

luna: Even after disbelief, “to Him is your return” and He will inform you of your deeds (إِلَيْهِ مَرْجِعُكُمْ); the verse preserves the order of return then account. | terra: The ayah addresses disbelief and gratitude, then says the return is to the Lord and He will inform people of what they did; response, return, and account remain linked.
terra: Affliction makes a person call on the Lord while turning penitently to Him, but relief is followed by forgetting and disbelief; the ayah exposes unstable, reversible orientation.
luna: Those who avoid false gods and turn back to God (أَنَابُوا إِلَى اللَّهِ) receive good news; the ayah gives a concrete favorable voluntary return.
terra: Earlier peoples denied, so punishment came upon them from where they did not perceive; unseen arrival realizes the threat carried by غاشية.
terra: The Prophet receives the Book for humanity; guidance or error belongs to each person and he is not their trustee, clarifying noncoercive reminder.

luna: People are commanded to turn back to their Lord before punishment comes (أَنِيبُوا إِلَىٰ رَبِّكُمْ); this gives the voluntary return its urgent, still-open moment. | terra: People are commanded to turn penitently to their Lord and submit before punishment comes; this is the voluntary return the section sets against compulsory return.
terra: Following revelation is urged before punishment comes suddenly and unnoticed, continuing the opportunity for voluntary return in 39:54.
terra: At punishment a soul wishes for another return so it might do good; this belated “return” defines the deadline implicit in the command of 39:54.

luna: On Resurrection Day, faces are blackened for those who lied about God (تَسْوَدُّ وُجُوهُهُم); it links denial to the adverse face-state. | terra: Those who lied about God are seen on Resurrection Day with darkened faces, letting disbelief appear in the face at the destination.
luna: The next ayah says God saves those who were mindful; it supplies the favorable counterpart to 39:60's blackened faces.
luna: The trumpet is blown, the dead fall, then it is blown again and they stand looking; this gives a concrete arrival and rising before the account.
luna: The earth shines, the record is placed, and prophets and witnesses are brought; this is the next stage of the accounting scene after 39:68.
luna: Every soul is fully repaid for what it did; this completes 39:69's record-and-witness scene.

luna: The source-section root ح س ب is used here: Each soul is repaid for what it earned with no injustice, and God is swift in account (سَرِيعُ الْحِسَابِ); it makes the accounting in 88:26 concrete. | terra: On that Day every soul is repaid for what it earned, without injustice, and God is swift in account; it states the character of the reckoning after return.
terra: The believer states that everyone's return is to God and that the transgressors are companions of the Fire, joining common return to divergent receptions.
terra: Whether the Messenger is shown part of the promise or taken in death, the opponents will be returned to God; the outcome does not depend on what the Prophet witnesses.
terra: The Quran gives good news and warning, yet most turn away and do not hear; it stages the failed reception of the prophetic reminder.
terra: The ungrateful person doubts the Hour, imagines a favorable return, but is promised disclosure of deeds and severe punishment; false confidence cannot cancel return or account.
terra: When favored, the human turns away and withdraws to his side; beside 41:50 it connects the bodily gesture of abandoning nearness to mistaken ideas about return.
terra: God chooses and guides to Himself the one who turns penitently; willing return is presented as a path of guidance.
terra: Those whom God lets stray have no protector and, on seeing punishment, ask whether there is any way of return; the possible return of life has become impossible.
terra: Those exposed to the Fire are humbled by abasement and look furtively, a final posture of those who lost themselves.

luna: The source-section act of turning away appears here as أعرضوا: if people turn away, the Prophet is not their guardian and has only to convey, matching 88:21-23's reminder and limit. | terra: If they turn away, the Prophet was not sent as their guardian and is charged only with delivery; the same response and limit on prophetic control are explicit.
luna: Whoever turns away from the remembrance (يَعْشُ عَن ذِكْرِ الرَّحْمَٰنِ) is assigned a satanic companion; it gives a specific consequence for turning away from remembrance.
terra: Pharaoh's people are seized with punishment so that they might return, another direct instance of preliminary punishment serving return before the end.

luna: The source-section root ء ت ي appears in the warning that the Hour may come suddenly while people are unaware, another direct arrival formulation. | terra: They await only the Hour coming suddenly while they do not perceive, closely repeating the sudden-arrival half of 12:107.
terra: The commanded watch is for a day when heaven comes with visible smoke, supplying the arrival in a two-ayah covering scene.
terra: The smoke of 44:10 covers the people and is named a painful punishment, showing a coming thing becoming an enveloping affliction.
terra: A clarifying messenger had already come to them, establishing the arrival to which their turning in the next ayah responds.
terra: After the messenger's coming in 44:13, they turn away from him and accuse him; it stages arrival followed immediately by aversion.
terra: God gives life, causes death, and then gathers everyone on the unquestionable Day; life's movement is gathered into a single return.

luna: Every nation is brought to its record and told it is repaid for what it did; this is a public scene of the reckoning that follows return. | terra: Every community is seen kneeling and summoned to its record, staging the posture and documentary summons of final account.
terra: God's record speaks truth and preserves what people did, explaining the evidentiary basis of the account in 45:28.

luna: The source-section root ء ت ي appears in the question whether they wait for the Hour to come suddenly; signs have already come, so refusal does not stop arrival. | terra: They await only the Hour to come suddenly, although its signs have already come; anticipated arrival and prior arrivals are juxtaposed.

luna: Some turn back after guidance has become clear (ارْتَدُّوا عَلَىٰ أَدْبَارِهِمْ); this is a reversal from guidance rather than the final return to God. | terra: Those who turn back on their heels after guidance is clear are enticed and given false hopes; their backward motion is a chosen reversal after recognition.
terra: When angels take the disbelievers in death, they strike their faces and backs; the gesture of refusal is overtaken at the boundary of return.
luna: The deniers call the return “far away” (رَجْعٌ بَعِيدٌ), the explicit contrary claim against the section's certainty that return is to God.
terra: Created signs are an insight and reminder for every penitent servant, joining reminder's efficacy to an already returning orientation.
luna: The trumpet is blown and the threatened Day arrives; this is the immediate setup for the arriving soul and lifted cover in 50:21-22.

luna: Every soul comes accompanied by a driver and a witness; the arrival is directly staged as a person is brought to account. | terra: Every soul comes accompanied by a driver and witness, staging the compulsory arrival that turns into judgment.
luna: The cover is removed from a person's sight (فَكَشَفْنَا عَنكَ غِطَاءَكَ); after the source's covering image, this is the judgment-day unveiling that ends concealment.

luna: The source-section root ء و ب is used here: Paradise is brought near for every “returning, guarding” person (أَوَّابٍ حَفِيظٍ); awāb is the very source-section form for one who repeatedly returns to God. | terra: Paradise is what was promised to every أَوَّاب, one repeatedly returning, and guardian; the named voluntary branch of the root is attached to its good destination.

luna: The God-fearing person “comes with a heart turning” (وَجَاءَ بِقَلْبٍ مُّنِيبٍ); arrival and inward voluntary return meet in one phrase. | terra: The promised person fears the Merciful unseen and comes with a penitent heart, combining chosen inward return with actual arrival.

luna: The section's claim that the return destination is fixed is repeated in “to Us is the final destination” (إِلَيْنَا الْمَصِيرُ). | terra: God gives life and death and “to Us is the destination”; the first-person divine destination directly parallels “to Us is their return.”
terra: The Prophet is not a compeller over them and must remind by the Quran whoever fears the warning; it is a near-parallel to 88:21-22 and its receptive addressee.
terra: The report of Abraham's honored guests is asked as something that has come to the Prophet, another direct instance of news arriving.
terra: Pharaoh turns away with his supporting power and dismisses Moses, a political and bodily enactment of abandoning the messenger's nearness.
terra: What covers the lote tree covers it, another pure covering use that helps preserve the distinction behind the section's coming gloss.

luna: The source-section root و ل ي is used here: The Prophet is told to turn from the one who turns away from the reminder and wants only worldly life (تَوَلَّىٰ عَن ذِكْرِنَا); the preposition and sense match the section's dictionary note. | terra: The Prophet is told to turn from the one who has turned from God's reminder and desires only the nearer life; reciprocal distance follows the hearer's first refusal.
luna: A person has only what he strives for (وَأَن لَّيْسَ لِلْإِنسَانِ إِلَّا مَا سَعَىٰ); the image's satisfied face in 88:9 follows from its effort.
luna: The next ayah says that the effort will be seen, supplying the disclosure before recompense.
luna: The next ayah says the effort will then be fully recompensed, linking 88:9's satisfaction to return and account.
terra: The final endpoint is to the Lord; this nonlexical formulation states why neither facing nor turning away can alter where movement ends.
luna: The source-section root غ ش و appears as the overturned townships are covered by what covered them (فَغَشَّاهَا مَا غَشَّىٰ); the word's covering sense is staged as punishment.
luna: The Hour has drawn near (اقْتَرَبَتِ السَّاعَةُ), another direct formulation of the approaching event that opens the image.
luna: When people see a sign they turn away (يُعْرِضُوا); the next ayah identifies this as a refusal of evidence, joining a sign's arrival to turning away.
luna: They deny and follow their desires (كَذَّبُوا وَاتَّبَعُوا أَهْوَاءَهُمْ); this completes 54:2's act of turning away with denial and its eventual settlement.
terra: The Prophet is commanded to turn away from them until the caller summons people to something terrible; here prophetic withdrawal awaits their compulsory response.
terra: With humbled eyes people emerge from graves and move toward the caller, a compulsory bodily response on the Day of return.
terra: Criminals are dragged on their faces into the Fire, making the final direction imposed rather than chosen.
terra: Hypocrites are told to “go back” and seek light, but a wall is then set between them and the believers; the commanded return exposes that the earlier opportunity has passed.
terra: God raises everyone, informs them of their deeds, and has counted what they forgot; resurrection culminates in exact disclosure and account.
terra: Abraham's prayer holds voluntary turning and final destination together: “to You we have turned” and “to You is the destination.”
terra: The death from which people flee will meet them, after which they are returned to the Knower and informed of their deeds; turning away cannot alter arrival, return, or reckoning.
terra: When death comes, a soul asks for a short delay to give and become righteous; the appeal reveals a return to action sought too late.
terra: God will not delay a soul once its appointed time comes, closing the requested interval of 63:10.
terra: The news of former disbelievers is asked as something that came to the hearers, and that news includes the evil consequence they tasted.
terra: Clear messengers came to earlier peoples, but they disbelieved and turned away (كَفَرُوا وَتَوَلَّوا); arrival of warning and the response of 88:23 are joined directly.
terra: The turners of 64:6 deny resurrection, but are told they will certainly be raised and informed of their deeds; this completes their unavoidable return and account.
terra: Obedience is commanded, but if people turn away the Messenger's task is only clear delivery; freedom to turn and responsibility for it remain distinct.
terra: A town that defiantly turned from its Lord's command and messengers was called to a severe account, joining refusal directly to reckoning.
terra: The town of 65:8 tastes the evil result of its conduct and ends in loss, supplying the consequence of its severe account.
luna: Hell's keepers ask whether a warner came; this sets up the warning-and-response scene that parallels the image's arriving report.
luna: The people admit a warner came but they denied him; this row's own contribution is the arrival of warning followed by rejection.
luna: They say that if they had listened or reasoned, they would not be among the Fire's inhabitants; this gives their turning away its stated cause.
luna: They confess their sin and are far from salvation; this completes the rejected-warning sequence with accountability.
luna: Those who fear their Lord unseen receive forgiveness and great reward, the favorable counterpart to the rejecters in 67:9-11.
terra: People are told to walk through the earth and eat God's provision, but to Him is the resurrection; ordinary movement across the world terminates in return.
terra: When the promised event is seen near, the disbelievers' faces become distressed; arrival is registered visibly on the face.
terra: Their eyes are humbled and abasement covers them, though in life they were called to prostrate while able; final posture answers earlier refusal.
luna: People are exposed on that Day and nothing hidden remains; this reverses the covering named by the source-section's root غ ش و.
luna: The favorable person receives their record in the right hand; this begins the two-sided account scene after 69:18's exposure.
luna: The favorable person says they expected to meet their account (إِنِّي ظَنَنتُ أَنِّي مُلَاقٍ حِسَابِيَهْ); the source-section's root ح س ب is explicit.
luna: The other person is given the record in the left hand, contrasting with the favorable record in 69:19.
luna: The person says they did not know what their account was (وَلَمْ أَدْرِ مَا حِسَابِيَهْ); this continues the adverse reckoning with the source-section root ح س ب.
luna: People see the Day as far away (إِنَّهُمْ يَرَوْنَهُ بَعِيدًا), contrasting their distance from the punishment with the source's nearer opportunity to return.
luna: God sees the same Day as near (وَنَرَاهُ قَرِيبًا); this completes the contrast in 70:6.

luna: The source-section root و ل ي is used here: The Fire calls the one who turned his back and turned away (أَدْبَرَ وَتَوَلَّىٰ); the doubled retreat gives a vivid counterpart to the inescapable return. | terra: The blaze calls the one who turned his back and turned away (أَدْبَرَ وَتَوَلَّى); the fugitive gesture itself cannot keep punishment from summoning him.
terra: They rush from graves with humbled eyes while abasement covers them, realizing the Day they had been promised.
terra: Whoever turns from the Lord's reminder is made to enter mounting punishment, attaching aversion from remembrance to its destination.

luna: After reflecting on the reminder, the opponent turns his back and grows arrogant (ثُمَّ أَدْبَرَ وَاسْتَكْبَرَ); it is a specific refusal-response scene. | terra: After considering the revelation, the opponent turns his back and acts arrogantly; the bodily turn is the decisive movement toward the punishment later named in the passage.
terra: The human asks “where is the escape?” on Resurrection Day, exposing the impulse to flee just before 75:12 names the settled destination.
terra: The answer “no refuge” closes off evasion and prepares the declaration that the destination is the Lord.

luna: The source defines awb as returning to one's settled place; “to your Lord that day is the settled destination” (إِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ يَوْمَئِذٍ الْمُسْتَقَرُّ) gives a close semantic parallel. | terra: On that Day the settled destination (ٱلْمُسْتَقَرُّ) is to the Lord, closely matching the dictionary description of return to one's place of settlement.
luna: On that Day a person is informed of what they sent ahead and left behind; this continues the settled destination in 75:12 with the disclosure/account that follows return.
luna: The next ayah says a person is a witness against themself, making the account self-evident after 75:13.
luna: Even if a person offers excuses, the account stands; this completes 75:14's self-witness scene.

luna: The source-section root و ج ه is used here: The Day's faces are radiant (وُجُوهٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ نَّاضِرَةٌ), a parallel to the contrasting faces and outcomes surrounding 88:2. | terra: Some faces on that Day are radiant, beginning a two-sided face scene parallel to the two groups of faces in surah 88.

luna: Those faces look toward their Lord (إِلَىٰ رَبِّهَا نَاظِرَةٌ); this gives the radiant face in 75:22 a directed, hopeful orientation. | terra: Those radiant faces look toward their Lord, making the blessed face's orientation explicit.

luna: The source-section root و ج ه is used here: The other faces are gloomy (وُجُوهٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ بَاسِرَةٌ), a direct contrary face-state to the radiant group and to 88:8-9. | terra: Other faces on that Day are grim, opening the opposed facial condition just as 88:2 stands against 88:8.

luna: The gloomy faces expect a backbreaking calamity; this next ayah completes the unfavorable face-state introduced in 75:24. | terra: The grim faces expect a crushing calamity, connecting the visible face to its anticipated end.
terra: “To your Lord that day is the driving” makes the destination unavoidable immediately before the passage describes the person who denied and turned away.
terra: The person “denied and turned away” (كَذَّبَ وَتَوَلَّى), echoing 88:23, within a scene whose stated destination is the Lord in 75:30.
terra: After denying and turning away, the person goes back to his family swaggering; apparent departure toward home occurs inside a passage that says the driving is to the Lord.
luna: Whoever wills may take a path to his Lord (اتَّخَذَ إِلَىٰ رَبِّهِ سَبِيلًا); it concretizes choosing a direction of return.

luna: The source-section root ء و ب gives the return-word ma'ab; here it names the destination for transgressors (مَآبًا), beside 78:39's chosen way to the Lord. | terra: Hell is “a place of return” (مَآبًا) for the transgressors, supplying the first of the section's two opposed destinations.

luna: The source-section root ء و ب is used here: The source-section's secondary sense of awāb as a willing return to God is made an explicit choice: whoever wills may take a return to his Lord (مَآبًا). | terra: On the true Day, whoever wills may take toward the Lord a مَآبًا; the same return noun becomes a voluntarily chosen way rather than the transgressors' destination in 78:22.
luna: The next ayah warns of a near punishment and the day each person will see what their hands sent ahead; it completes 78:39's chosen return with its stakes.
terra: Eyes are humbled amid the resurrection terror, closely echoing the humbled faces at the opening of surah 88's judgment scene.
terra: The same question about Moses' report coming to the Prophet confirms the section's reading of أَتَىٰكَ as the arrival of news.
terra: Pharaoh denies and disobeys, supplying the moral content of the turn described in the next ayah.
terra: Pharaoh then turns his back and strives, an enacted departure whose destination is the divine seizure in 79:25.
terra: God seizes Pharaoh with an exemplary punishment for the last and first offenses, completing the path begun by his back-turning in 79:22.
luna: The greatest catastrophe comes (فَإِذَا جَاءَتِ الطَّامَّةُ الْكُبْرَىٰ), another arrival-form for the overwhelming Day.
luna: On that Day a person remembers what they strove for; it supplies the response to the catastrophe arriving in 79:34.
luna: The Fire is exposed for those who see; this completes the arrival scene with the adverse outcome.

luna: The source-section root و ل ي is used here: The Prophet “turned away” (تَوَلَّىٰ) from a seeker; unlike 88:23's disbelieving refusal, this different stance shows that the verb itself names turning away, while context determines its moral force. | terra: The Prophet himself turns away from the blind visitor and is corrected; this bounds the root's moral force, since the gesture is not disbelief yet still carries responsibility.
luna: The blind man had come to the Prophet (جَاءَهُ الْأَعْمَىٰ); his arrival completes 80:1's striking scene of someone coming as another turns away.

luna: The source-section root و ج ه is used here: The other surah's final scene begins with faces bright and shining (وُجُوهٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ مُّسْفِرَةٌ), paralleling the two face-groups of al-Ghashiya. | terra: Faces on that Day are bright, beginning another direct counterpart to surah 88's contrasting faces.

luna: Those bright faces are laughing and joyful (ضَاحِكَةٌ مُّسْتَبْشِرَةٌ); this gives the favorable face in 80:38 its response. | terra: Their laughing and rejoicing completes the blessed face's visible condition.

luna: The source-section root و ج ه is used here: The contrasting faces are covered in dust (وُجُوهٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ عَلَيْهَا غَبَرَةٌ), a grim counterpart to the bright faces and to 88:2's humbled faces. | terra: Other faces on that Day bear dust, introducing the opposite group.

luna: Darkness overwhelms the dusty faces (تَرْهَقُهَا قَتَرَةٌ), completing the visual contrast begun in 80:40. | terra: Darkness covers those faces, joining the face contrast to the image of covering.
luna: The final ayah identifies this latter group as disbelieving, wicked people; it completes the face-scene's link between outward state and rejection.
luna: Each soul then knows what it sent ahead and left behind; this gives the reckoning after resurrection a specific act of disclosure.

luna: Every person labors toward the Lord and will meet Him (فَمُلَاقِيهِ); whatever their present direction, the meeting cannot be avoided. | terra: Every human is laboring step by step toward the Lord and will meet Him; this directly renders the section's claim that even apparent departure is movement toward return.

luna: The next verses begin the outcome of that meeting with a person given the record in the right hand; this row contributes the favorable recipient in the accounting scene. | terra: The favorable recipient is given his record in his right hand, identifying the person whose return proceeds to the easy account in 84:8.

luna: The source-section root ح س ب appears in this person's easy reckoning (حِسَابًا يَسِيرًا), a direct counterpart to the account laid upon God in 88:26. | terra: The person given his record in his right hand receives an easy account; after the meeting in 84:6, the return proceeds to precisely the reckoning named in 88:26.
luna: After that reckoning, the person returns to their family joyful (يَنقَلِبُ إِلَىٰ أَهْلِهِ مَسْرُورًا), joining return with the glad state of 88:9.

luna: The contrasting recipient is given the record behind his back (وَرَاءَ ظَهْرِهِ), making bodily reversal part of the unfavorable accounting scene. | terra: The other recipient is given his record from behind his back; the turned back becomes the place where the evidence of account reaches him.

luna: The person given the record behind his back calls for destruction; this is the next consequence after the unfavorable account begun in 84:10. | terra: The recipient of the record behind his back calls for destruction, beginning the consequence of the backward-facing account scene.

luna: The sequence ends with entry into the Blaze, completing the punished return that contrasts with 84:9's joyful return. | terra: He enters a blazing fire, completing the destination attached to the record delivered behind his back.
terra: The doomed person thought he would never return (أَن لَّن يَحُورَ), exposing as delusion the belief that turning one's back changes the destination.
terra: The answer to his belief that he would not return is that his Lord always saw him, so denial of return never removed him from divine sight.
terra: The report of the hosts is likewise phrased as having come to the Prophet, repeating the verbal scene of 88:1.
terra: The command to remind when reminder benefits supplies the same prophetic act that immediately precedes the turning away in surah 88.
terra: The person who fears will take the reminder, identifying the responsive hearer of the command in 87:9 and contrasting the one who turns away.
luna: The Lord comes with the angels in ranks (وَجَاءَ رَبُّكَ وَالْمَلَكُ صَفًّا صَفًّا), a distinct final-arrival scene beside al-Ghashiya's arrival.

luna: This neighboring call identifies the addressee as the reassured soul (النَّفْسُ الْمُطْمَئِنَّةُ), explaining why 89:28's return is welcomed. | terra: The tranquil soul is addressed before being commanded to return, identifying the inward state capable of the willing return in 89:28.

luna: The return becomes an invitation to a willing soul: “Return to your Lord” (ارْجِعِي إِلَىٰ رَبِّكِ), pleased and pleasing, matching the section's voluntary branch of return. | terra: The tranquil soul is told to return to its Lord content and pleasing; this directly joins voluntary return to the satisfaction evoked by 88:9.

luna: After the return in 89:28, the soul is told to enter among God's servants (فَادْخُلِي فِي عِبَادِي); this completes the destination's welcome. | terra: After returning contentedly, the soul is told to enter among God's servants, specifying the company into which that return leads.

luna: The next command is to enter God's Garden (وَادْخُلِي جَنَّتِي), completing the willing return's destination. | terra: The returning soul is told to enter God's garden, completing the favorable destination of the voluntary return.
terra: Night “when it covers” supplies the plain enveloping sense of the root غ ش و that the section sets beside its idiom of coming.
terra: The warning of a blazing fire supplies the punishment into which the denier who turns away in 92:16 enters.

luna: The source-section root و ل ي is used here: The wretched person is defined as one who denied and turned away (كَذَّبَ وَتَوَلَّىٰ), then is kept from the Fire's opposite; this closely matches the image's paired refusal and consequence. | terra: The one who enters the blazing fire is defined as the person who denied and turned away; its exact phrase mirrors 88:23 and fixes the consequence.
luna: The self-sufficient person transgresses (أَن رَّآهُ اسْتَغْنَىٰ); the next ayah's certain return overturns his imagined independence.

luna: The source's return to a settled destination is stated as “to your Lord is the return” (إِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ الرُّجْعَىٰ), countering any idea that turning away changes where one ends. | terra: After the human deems himself self-sufficient and transgresses, this ayah answers that the return is to the Lord, so imagined independence cannot change the endpoint.
terra: People issue forth in separate groups to be shown their deeds, a scene in which final movement culminates in disclosure.

luna: Whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it; this is a precise favorable result of the account after return. | terra: Even an atom's weight of good is seen, specifying the exactness of the account reached in 99:6.

luna: Whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it; it supplies the adverse counterpart to 99:7. | terra: Even an atom's weight of evil is seen, completing the two-sided precision of that account.
